keptBefore.name: Hester Lake Route
hazards: Avalanche potential on the upper ridge gullies in spring snow conditions.
Boggy, slick trail sections (skunk-cabbage wetlands) near the Hester Lakes.
Loose rock in the boulder field below the east ridge.
keptBefore.overview: A longer wilderness approach up Mount Price's south/east side via the Hester Lake basin, gaining the peak's east ridge by a boulder-field scramble and finishing along a steep, partly snow-and-rock ridge to the summit.
keptBefore.beta: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, follow the Dingford Creek Trail (multiple creek crossings) toward Hester Lake and Little Hester Lake — roughly the first 5-6 miles. From the lakes basin, ascend the boulder field south of Little Hester Lake to gain Price's east ridge near Point 5,480'/5,440', traverse the steep north side of the ridge to a col around 5,400 ft just east of the true summit, and finish with a short ridge scramble to the 5,587 ft summit. Expect Class 3 scrambling with occasional steep snow or rock gullies on the ridge, and real routefinding difficulty — at least one party's own GPS track diverged noticeably between ascent and descent.
keptBefore.turnaround: Given the brush, creek crossings, and off-trail routefinding on both approach and descent, set a conservative turnaround time — parties have finished this route after dark.
keptBefore.face: South/East flank via Hester Lake basin and east ridge
keptBefore.descent: Descend the same general line back through the boulder field and Hester Lake basin to the Dingford Creek Trail; several parties report their descent line diverging from the ascent for lack of a fixed route.
obj_haz: Steep, loose gully on Price Creek (3,200-3,800 ft) — the route's technical crux
Devil's club and heavy brush below ~4,000 ft when snow-free
Cliff bands around Hester Lake / Little Hester Lake requiring detours
Steep snow or rock gullies on the upper east ridge (Class 3)
Avalanche potential on the upper gullies in spring conditions

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 34, turn north on 468th Ave SE and in about 0.6 mile turn right onto the Middle Fork Road (FR 56). Follow it about 12 miles to the Taylor River junction, stay right on the Middle Fork Road, and continue roughly 6 miles on rougher road to the Dingford Creek Trailhead at about 1,400 ft, with parking on the right. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and higher clearance helps on the last stretch.

waypoints.name: Mount Price Summit
waypoints.directions: Climb Dingford Creek Trail 1005 past Pumpkinseed Falls and several stream crossings to the fork at about 3 miles, bear right on the Hester Lake Trail, and gain about 1,000 ft in 2.5 miles to Hester Lake. Continue to Little Hester Lake and climb the boulder field directly south of it to Price's east ridge, east of the 5,440-ft subpeak. Traverse the steep north side of the ridge to the 5,400-ft col just east of the summit, then scramble the final ridge to the top.

keptBefore.detailed_rack: No fixed protection; a rope/light rack could be carried by less experienced parties for the steeper ridge sections, though most parties scramble it unroped.
what_to_bring: Map/GPS with a saved track (routefinding is difficult and reported unreliable even with GPS)
Extra layers/food for a long day
Gaiters (boggy, brushy trail sections near the lakes)
Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Pass
Free self-issue wilderness permit (Alpine Lakes Wilderness, May 15-Oct 31)
ice axe — useful for the Price Creek gully and upper ridge when snow-covered
pro_tips: Carry a GPS track from a prior trip report if possible — at least one party's own GPS failed mid-climb and their documented ascent line proved suboptimal.
In early October, running water can be found beneath the boulders a few hundred feet above Little Hester Lake, a handy refill before the long walk out.
watch_out: Devil's club and heavy brush below about 4,000 ft when snow-free.
Log crossings of Dingford Creek and side creeks on the approach.
Steep snow or rock gullies on the upper ridge — Class 3 max but exposed.
Cliff bands around Hester Lake and Little Hester Lake requiring careful routefinding.
Long day with real risk of finishing after dark.
In early October the shaded boulder slope south of Little Hester Lake is coated in wet moss and slick underfoot.
keptBefore.pro_needs: None fixed — unroped scramble; steep snow sections may warrant an axe and, in early season, crampons/microspikes.
keptBefore.best_season: accounts differ on the ideal window: some recommend climbing while snow still covers the lower slopes to avoid heavy brush and devil's club below 4,000 ft, while others prefer late-summer conditions (roughly July-September) when the gullies are scree rather than avalanche-prone snow. Either way, expect some bushwhacking low and possible steep snow high into early summer.
keptBefore.approach: Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) to the Dingford Creek Trailhead (~1,400 ft). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail, crossing several creeks, toward the Hester Lake basin (roughly 5-6 miles) before leaving the trail to begin the off-trail scramble.
keptBefore.descent_text: From the summit, reverse the final ridge scramble to the ~5,400 ft col, traverse back across the steep north side of the east ridge, and downclimb the boulder field to the Hester Lake / Little Hester Lake basin. Pick up the Dingford Creek Trail near the lakes and follow it back to the trailhead. Expect brush, including devil's club, below about 4,000 ft when the route is snow-free; allow extra time — one documented trip took over 10 hours car-to-car.
keptBefore.bail: Retreat down the ascent line to the Hester Lake basin and back onto the maintained Dingford Creek Trail from any point; there are no fixed anchors or rappels on this route.

pitch_detail.notes: Boulder field south of Little Hester Lake up the east ridge (near Pt. 5,480'/5,440'), traverse to the ~5,400 ft col, final ridge scramble to the 5,587 ft summit.

keptBefore.itinerary: Full, often long day: Dingford Creek TH -> ~5-6 mi trail to the Hester Lake basin -> off-trail gully/boulder-field/ridge scramble to the summit -> reverse descent. At least one trip report logged roughly 10.5 hours car-to-car; start early and carry a headlamp.

May.reason: Snow covers the brush below 4,000 ft, but the upper ridge gullies are still avalanche-prone and Dingford's creek crossings run high.

July.reason: The ridge gullies melt out to scree, the boggy Hester Lake trail dries out, and the north-side ridge traverse is snow-free.

June.reason: Lingering snow smooths the boulder field and brush but can still load the steep gullies; the Price Creek gully is wet and slick.

August.reason: Dry rock on the east ridge and the Point 5,480 bypass, though the devil's club and brush below 4,000 ft are at their thickest.

October.reason: Fall rain turns the skunk-cabbage wetlands to mud and wets the talus, and the first snow can reach the ridge.

September.reason: Cooler, drier days on the boulder field, but short days and early rain make the heather and talus slippery.

bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
bivy.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is cut by a washout at milepost 17.3 that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft; the Forest Service's road-damage alert of June 30, 2026 lists it with no reopening date. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

before.name: East Route
watch_out: By mid-October patches of slushy snow start near 5,000 ft and two steep snowfields below the ridge call for an ice axe.
before.approach: Start at the Rachel Lake trailhead at the end of the Box Canyon road (FR 4930) and walk Rachel Lake Trail #1313 for about 2.2 miles, passing a brushy avalanche clearing where the summit block shows ahead. Just beyond it, watch on the right for the unmarked climbers' boot path that climbs steeply through timber and deadfall, mostly Class 2. It breaks out below a cliff band: pass the first cliffs on the right, work left around a rock outcrop, and take a gully on the right through the second cliffs. The path then leads up to the open slopes at about 6,250 ft below the summit block, where the East Route splits off to the right around the south and east sides. Expect roughly 3,800 to 3,900 ft of gain from the car.
before.descent_text: Descend the way you came. From the summit, downclimb the east-side gully and the low-exposure Class 3 cleft, then head back across the base of the summit block to the top of the boot path. Follow it down through both cliff bands, using the same gully on the right, and stay on the existing tread rather than cutting new lines through the loose scree. Watch for the exit where the boot path meets Rachel Lake Trail near the avalanche clearing; it is easy to miss in the trees. From there it is an easy walk of a little over two miles to the trailhead. No rappel is needed.

keptBefore.name: Standard Scramble
hazards: exposed Class 3 notch/chimney on the summit block
loose talus and scree above ~4,600 ft on Box Ridge's south face, with real rockfall risk onto parties below
a deceptive gully on the SW side of the summit block that cliffs out at Class 4 — a common wrong-turn trap; stay climber's right of it

keptBefore.overview: Hibox Mountain (6,548 ft) is the high point of Box Ridge, a rugged sub-ridge of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness about 5 miles east of Snoqualmie Pass, rising above the popular Rachel Lake basin. It's one of the most-climbed scrambles near I-90, combining an easy trail approach with a steep, loose Class 2-3 boot path up Box Ridge and a short, exposed Class 3 summit block. Summit views take in Rampart Ridge, Alta Mountain, Three Queens, Mount Thompson, Rachel Lake, and the Stuart Range.
keptBefore.beta: From the Rachel Lake trailhead, follow the maintained Rachel Lake Trail for roughly 2 miles to the first avalanche-chute clearing. A boot path for Hibox leaves the main trail here (or at the second chute crossing) and climbs steeply but stays class 2 through timber to near treeline. Above the trees, go right around the first band of cliffs, then left around a rock outcrop, continue through more timber to a second cliff band, and take the gully on the right to gain the upper mountain. From there head right (east) along the south side of the summit rocks to a gully on the east side, which is climbed with a bit of class 3 near the top to reach the summit. Route-finding is the main challenge; there is no continuous trail above the boot path.
keptBefore.turnaround: Turn around at the summit block if exposure feels beyond your comfort.
keptBefore.rappels: None; the route is down-climbed via the same line as the ascent.
keptBefore.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
keptBefore.descent: Reverse the boot path down Box Ridge to Rachel Lake, then out the Rachel Lake Trail to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Rachel Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 62 (Kachess Lake), turn left off the ramp and follow FR 49 (Kachess Lake Road) toward Kachess Lake. Follow the signs toward Lake Kachess Campground and turn left on FR 4930 (Box Canyon Road), which ends at a large lot and the Rachel Lake trailhead about 4 miles from the turn, around 2,800 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, plus a free self-issue wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Hibox Mountain Summit
waypoints.directions: Follow Rachel Lake Trail #1313 about 2 miles to a brushy avalanche clearing near 3,300 ft; just past it take the unmarked climbers' path uphill on the right. Pass the first cliff band on the right, go left around an outcrop, and take a gully on the right through the second band. Climb the meadow and talus to the south side of the summit block, traverse east to the east-side gully, and climb its short class 3 notch to the top.

keptBefore.detailed_rack: No real rack; a short rope and a sling optional for the exposed summit block.
pro_tips: Bring a helmet for the whole talus/boot-path section, not just the summit block — rockfall from parties above is a known hazard

If you lose the boot path near the avalanche clearings past Rachel Lake, backtrack rather than bushwhacking blind — the real trail reappears under tree canopy a short distance past the obvious false path
Keep climber's right of the gully below the summit block on both ascent and descent; it cliffs out at Class 4 and is a frequent source of epics
watch_out: The correct boot path junction beyond Rachel Lake is easy to miss — a false trail through brush appears first; keep going until you're back under tree canopy to find the real path
Don't be lured into the SW gully below the summit block — it cliffs out at Class 4/5; the standard line stays climber's right
Loose talus above 4,600 ft sheds rock easily; space parties out and wear a helmet the whole way up, not just at the summit block
keptBefore.best_season: July through early October; snow can linger in the upper gully and basin into July in heavy-snowpack years
keptBefore.approach: Start at the Rachel Lake Trailhead (Trail #1313, elev. ~2,800 ft) at the end of Box Canyon Road/FR-4930. Follow the Rachel Lake Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the Box Canyon Creek drainage — the grade is easy and well-graded here, mostly Class 1 hiking. At roughly 2–2.2 miles and about 450–500 ft of gain (~3,300 ft elevation), the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing where Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast; this clearing is the key landmark. Just past it (some parties note it's after the second such clearing), watch on the right/climber's-right side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path (the 'Hibox climbers' path') leaving the maintained trail and heading northeast/uphill into the forest — it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. From here the character changes completely: the bootpath climbs steeply (mostly Class 2, with fallen timber to step over) before breaking out of the trees near a band of cliffs around 5,300 ft. Stay right of this first rock band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continuing through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band; a gully on the right provides passage through it. Above this the trail opens into a large sloping subalpine meadow (wildflowers in season) that funnels into a loose talus/scree slope — this is the most tedious and slip-prone section of the route, so careful foot placement matters more than pace. A thready boot path threads up through the talus to the south side of the summit block. There is no reliable water past the lower forest/creek section, so carry what you need from the car or treat water low on the mountain. The route-finding through the two cliff bands and the avalanche-path junction low on the trail are the two spots parties most often go astray; a GPS track or recent trip report beta is worth having.
keptBefore.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than glissading the scree, which is loose and eroded. From the summit, downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block (good rock, low exposure, easy Class 3 moves), then pick your way back down through the loose talus/scree field to the sloping meadow. Some parties descend via a slightly different line on the east side of the summit block/east ridge before rejoining the ascent boot path lower down — functionally the same route, just avoid cutting new paths through the scree to limit erosion. Continue down through the two cliff bands (reversing right/left as on the way up) and back into the timber, staying alert for the boot path's exit point onto the maintained Rachel Lake Trail near the ~3,300 ft avalanche clearing — it's easy to miss in the trees when descending. Once back on Rachel Lake Trail #1313, it's an easy, well-graded 2+ miles back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required — the summit block's only technical move is a short, low-exposure Class 3 downclimb, not a rappel. Watch the weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in this range and parties often report hurrying off the loose upper slopes ahead of incoming storms.
keptBefore.bail: Reverse the boot path down Box Ridge to the Rachel Lake Trail and walk out the trail to the trailhead.

pitch_detail.notes: ~2 miles of maintained Rachel Lake Trail from the trailhead to the first avalanche-chute clearing.
Unmarked boot path leaves the main trail near the avalanche-chute crossing and climbs steeply through timber; stays class 2 to near the forest edge.
Go right around the first cliff band, left around a rock outcrop, through more timber to a second cliff band, then up a gully on the right to gain the upper mountain.

Traverse east along the south side of the summit rocks to a gully on the east side; climb it with a short class 3 section near the top to reach the true summit (map-measured up to ~47 degrees in the steepest section).

itinerary.cal: Snow-free and easiest roughly July through October; the boot path can hold snow into early summer in big years, so check recent trip reports before a June/early-July attempt.

days.note: Hike the Rachel Lake Trail to the first avalanche clearing, pick up the unmarked but well-used Hibox boot path climbing north up steep timber and talus on the slopes of Box Ridge to the south side of the summit block, then traverse east beneath it to the east-side gully and a short Class 3 scramble on solid rock to the summit. Reverse the same line to descend. Snow-free bootpath is easy to follow in summer season; the whole outing is a long single day, not an overnight.

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake Trail to the avalanche clearing, then the Hibox climbers' path over two cliff bands
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rachel Lake trailhead, Trail #1313, about 2,800 ft, at the end of Box Canyon Road / FR-4930. The trail climbs gently through forest along Box Canyon Creek, easy class 1 walking.

At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles and about 3,300 ft the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing. That clearing is the key landmark, because Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast from it.

Above the boot path the tread climbs steeply, mostly class 2 with fallen timber, about 500 vertical feet to a band of cliffs near 5,300 ft. Stay right of that first band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continue through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band, and take the gully on the right through it. Above, a large sloping subalpine meadow funnels into loose talus and scree.

No reliable water past the lower forest. About 5.6 km and 3,900 ft.

A deceptive gully on the southwest side of the summit block that cliffs out at class 4 — stay climbers' right of it
Loose talus and scree above about 4,600 ft with real rockfall risk onto parties below
An exposed class 3 notch and chimney on the summit block, whose downclimb is the part to think about before committing
Lingering snow and ice in the upper gully and basin into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The clearing is the first test and the summit block is its proof. At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles the maintained trail crosses a brushy avalanche clearing, and from it Hibox's summit block is visible on the ridge to the northeast. Just past that clearing — some parties say after the second such clearing — watch the right, climbers'-right, side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path heading northeast and uphill into the forest. It is easy to walk past if you are not looking.

The two cliff bands are a counted sequence, which is what you want in fog: first band, pass it on the right; then left around a rock outcrop; second band, take the gully on the right. Two bands, right then left then right. If you have passed only one band you are not yet on the upper mountain.

And here is the wrong-turn trap that matters most, at the top: the talus tops out on the south side of the summit block, and the rock straight above you there is steeper and more broken than it looks. That is the spot where parties commit to the wrong line, and there is a deceptive gully on the southwest side of the block that cliffs out at class 4. Do not climb what is above you.

What to do instead, which is the actual base finding: work right, staying along the south side of the rock and heading east, on loose talus over a sloping bed, until a reasonable gully opens on the east side of the block. That east gully is the route. It stays easy until the top, where a short notch or narrow chimney gives a bit of genuine class 3 on good, solid holds to a small summit platform.

And a descent note that belongs with the finding: the boot path through the brushy avalanche clearings is easy to lose on the way down, especially in fog. Look back at the junction on the way up.

climbing_route.label: South side of the summit block
climbing_route.notes: The talus slope tops out on the south side of the summit block. Do not try to climb the rock straight above you here — the direct south side is steeper and more broken than it looks, and it is the spot where parties commit to the wrong line. Instead line yourself up with the south side of the block and prepare to traverse.

climbing_route.label: Traverse east under the block
climbing_route.notes: Work right, staying along the south side of the rock and heading east, until a reasonable gully opens on the east side. The traverse is on loose talus and scree over a sloping bed — the most slip-prone ground on the route, where deliberate foot placement matters more than speed. It is also the last place to turn around easily.

climbing_route.label: East gully and summit notch
climbing_route.notes: Ascend the gully on the east side of the block. It stays easy until the top, where a short notch or narrow chimney runs up to the summit rock and gives a bit of genuine Class 3 scrambling. The rock here is reported as good and the holds solid, but the position is exposed and the summit itself is a small platform with steep ground on several sides. The downclimb of this last step is the part to think about before committing to it, and wet or icy rock changes the character of the notch entirely.

bivy.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
bivy.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
bivy.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

bivy.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
bivy.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
bivy.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
bivy.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

keptBefore.overview: Hibox Mountain (6,548 ft) is the high point of Box Ridge, a rugged sub-ridge of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness about 5 miles east of Snoqualmie Pass, rising above the popular Rachel Lake basin. It's one of the most-climbed scrambles near I-90, combining an easy trail approach with a steep, loose Class 2-3 boot path up Box Ridge and a short, exposed Class 3 summit block. Summit views take in Rampart Ridge, Alta Mountain, Three Queens, Mount Thompson, Rachel Lake, and the Stuart Range.
keptBefore.beta: From the Rachel Lake trailhead, follow the maintained Rachel Lake Trail for roughly 2 miles to the first avalanche-chute clearing. A boot path for Hibox leaves the main trail here (or at the second chute crossing) and climbs steeply but stays class 2 through timber to near treeline. Above the trees, go right around the first band of cliffs, then left around a rock outcrop, continue through more timber to a second cliff band, and take the gully on the right to gain the upper mountain. From there head right (east) along the south side of the summit rocks to a gully on the east side, which is climbed with a bit of class 3 near the top to reach the summit. Route-finding is the main challenge; there is no continuous trail above the boot path.
keptBefore.turnaround: Turn around at the summit block if exposure feels beyond your comfort.
keptBefore.rappels: None; the route is down-climbed via the same line as the ascent.
keptBefore.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
keptBefore.descent: Reverse the boot path down Box Ridge to Rachel Lake, then out the Rachel Lake Trail to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Hibox Mountain Summit
waypoints.directions: Follow Rachel Lake Trail #1313 about 2 miles to a brushy avalanche clearing near 3,300 ft; just past it take the unmarked climbers' path uphill on the right. Pass the first cliff band on the right, go left around an outcrop, and take a gully on the right through the second band. Climb the meadow and talus to the south side of the summit block, traverse east to the east-side gully, and climb its short class 3 notch to the top.

pro_tips: Bring a helmet for the whole talus/boot-path section, not just the summit block — rockfall from parties above is a known hazard

If you lose the boot path near the avalanche clearings past Rachel Lake, backtrack rather than bushwhacking blind — the real trail reappears under tree canopy a short distance past the obvious false path
Keep climber's right of the gully below the summit block on both ascent and descent; it cliffs out at Class 4 and is a frequent source of epics
watch_out: The correct boot path junction beyond Rachel Lake is easy to miss — a false trail through brush appears first; keep going until you're back under tree canopy to find the real path
Don't be lured into the SW gully below the summit block — it cliffs out at Class 4/5; the standard line stays climber's right
Loose talus above 4,600 ft sheds rock easily; space parties out and wear a helmet the whole way up, not just at the summit block
keptBefore.best_season: July through early October; snow can linger in the upper gully and basin into July in heavy-snowpack years
keptBefore.approach: Start at the Rachel Lake Trailhead (Trail #1313, elev. ~2,800 ft) at the end of Box Canyon Road/FR-4930. Follow the Rachel Lake Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the Box Canyon Creek drainage — the grade is easy and well-graded here, mostly Class 1 hiking. At roughly 2–2.2 miles and about 450–500 ft of gain (~3,300 ft elevation), the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing where Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast; this clearing is the key landmark. Just past it (some parties note it's after the second such clearing), watch on the right/climber's-right side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path (the 'Hibox climbers' path') leaving the maintained trail and heading northeast/uphill into the forest — it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. From here the character changes completely: the bootpath climbs steeply (mostly Class 2, with fallen timber to step over) before breaking out of the trees near a band of cliffs around 5,300 ft. Stay right of this first rock band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continuing through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band; a gully on the right provides passage through it. Above this the trail opens into a large sloping subalpine meadow (wildflowers in season) that funnels into a loose talus/scree slope — this is the most tedious and slip-prone section of the route, so careful foot placement matters more than pace. A thready boot path threads up through the talus to the south side of the summit block. There is no reliable water past the lower forest/creek section, so carry what you need from the car or treat water low on the mountain. The route-finding through the two cliff bands and the avalanche-path junction low on the trail are the two spots parties most often go astray; a GPS track or recent trip report beta is worth having.
keptBefore.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than glissading the scree, which is loose and eroded. From the summit, downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block (good rock, low exposure, easy Class 3 moves), then pick your way back down through the loose talus/scree field to the sloping meadow. Some parties descend via a slightly different line on the east side of the summit block/east ridge before rejoining the ascent boot path lower down — functionally the same route, just avoid cutting new paths through the scree to limit erosion. Continue down through the two cliff bands (reversing right/left as on the way up) and back into the timber, staying alert for the boot path's exit point onto the maintained Rachel Lake Trail near the ~3,300 ft avalanche clearing — it's easy to miss in the trees when descending. Once back on Rachel Lake Trail #1313, it's an easy, well-graded 2+ miles back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required — the summit block's only technical move is a short, low-exposure Class 3 downclimb, not a rappel. Watch the weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in this range and parties often report hurrying off the loose upper slopes ahead of incoming storms.
keptBefore.bail: Reverse the boot path down Box Ridge to the Rachel Lake Trail and walk out the trail to the trailhead.

pitch_detail.notes: ~2 miles of maintained Rachel Lake Trail from the trailhead to the first avalanche-chute clearing.
Unmarked boot path leaves the main trail near the avalanche-chute crossing and climbs steeply through timber; stays class 2 to near the forest edge.
Go right around the first cliff band, left around a rock outcrop, through more timber to a second cliff band, then up a gully on the right to gain the upper mountain.

itinerary.cal: Snow-free and easiest roughly July through October; the boot path can hold snow into early summer in big years, so check recent trip reports before a June/early-July attempt.

days.note: Hike the Rachel Lake Trail to the first avalanche clearing, pick up the unmarked but well-used Hibox boot path climbing north up steep timber and talus on the slopes of Box Ridge to the south side of the summit block, then traverse east beneath it to the east-side gully and a short Class 3 scramble on solid rock to the summit. set.beta: Follow the same climbers' path to the open slopes below the summit block, then bear right over loose talus and scree to meet the summit ridge near 6,300 ft, just southeast of the block. before.name: South Face
before.overview: Once up the chossy gully, find the flake heading up and right and follow it to the crest. Belay from good cracks on the higher slabs. From there, either pitch it out to the top or scramble. Could suit soloing as an alternative to the scramble up the back side.

keptBefore.overview: Iron Cap Mountain (6,347 ft) rises above the Williams Lake and La Bohn Gap country near the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Despite its modest elevation, it has striking local relief, climbing about 2,500 feet above the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Valley in less than a mile. The mountain straddles two drainages: its south side sheds into tributaries of the Snoqualmie River via the Williams Lake basin, while the north side drains toward the Foss River. It was first climbed in 1925 by a party led by Seattle mountaineer Joe Hazard. This route comes in from the north on the West Fork Foss River trail off US 2, past Trout, Copper and Big Heart lakes to a camp at Chetwoot Lake, and finishes on Iron Cap's west and north ridges.
keptBefore.beta: A long backcountry approach (6.6+ trail miles, ~3,400 ft gain to Chetwoot Lake) followed by off-trail cross-country travel and unroped class 3 scrambling on the west and north ridges. Solid granite in places but loose talus and scree lower down; most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a camp at Big Heart or Chetwoot Lake.
keptBefore.turnaround: Given the long approach and off-trail, unmarked ridge terrain, set a firm turnaround time before setting out and stick to it — losing daylight or getting caught by weather on the loose, exposed class 3 ridge or during cross-country travel back to the trail is the main risk on this route.
keptBefore.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
obj_haz: Small glacial remnant (locally called the 'Iron Cap Glacier') and lingering snow/ice on the peak's north side into summer
Loose talus and boulder terrain typical of Alpine Lakes Wilderness cross-country approaches

waypoints.name: West Fork Foss Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of the West Fork Foss Lakes Trail #1064 at the end of FR 6835. Self-issue the free Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the kiosk; a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park.
waypoints.directions: From US 2 about 1.9 miles east of Skykomish, turn south on Foss River Road (FR 68); the pavement ends at 1.2 miles. Stay right at the Y at 3.5 miles, and at 4.7 miles, just before a bridge, turn left onto FR 6835 (the sign is easy to miss) and drive 1.9 miles to the West Fork Foss trailhead at about 1,600 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park; self-issue the free wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Big Heart Lake (trail end)
waypoints.note: The maintained trail ends on the rocky rise above the lake's outlet, with established sites nearby; popular and often busy. From here the way on is cross-country over the south end of Atrium Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the West Fork Foss Lakes Trail #1064 past Trout Lake at 1.6 miles, then climb to Copper Lake at about 4.2 miles and continue past Little Heart Lake to Big Heart Lake at 7.3 miles, where the maintained trail ends on the rocky rise above the outlet.

waypoints.name: Chetwoot Lake camp
waypoints.note: Camps near the lake's east-end outlet, just south of Little Chetwoot Lake; quieter than Big Heart. The climb heads up talus and heather toward Point 6077 from here.
waypoints.directions: Go cross-country south over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake, to the camps near Chetwoot Lake's east-end outlet. Cairns are sparse through the boulder fields, so carry a map or GPS track.

waypoints.name: Iron Cap Mountain
waypoints.directions: Climb talus and heather toward Point 6077, pass it on the east, and gain the west ridge for easy Class 3 scrambling. Downclimb a short third-class step into a notch, then follow the wide ramp below the summit block to the broad north ridge and easy red-tinged rock and dirt to the summit.

Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit (available at the trailhead)

pro_tips: Many parties climb Iron Cap as part of a longer traverse (Big Snow Mountain, Chetwoot/Tank Lakes, La Bohn Gap) rather than as an isolated day trip, since the approach is so long
Water is plentiful at the lakes along the approach but scarce on the ridge above Chetwoot and Iron Cap lakes; fill up before the climb
Big Heart Lake is a popular, busy destination; the camps beyond it at Chetwoot Lake are much quieter

The 3rd-class downclimb to the crux notch is a bit exposed; take care with a loaded pack

keptBefore.pro_needs: No technical protection is needed — this is an unroped class 3 scramble on talus and blocky rock.
keptBefore.approach: Start at the West Fork Foss River trailhead (~1,650 ft): from US 2 at Skykomish, turn south on Foss River Road (FR 68), then left on FR 6835 (signed for Trail 1064) for its last 1.9 miles to the trailhead. Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permits are at the trailhead. The West Fork Foss Lakes Trail #1064 reaches Trout Lake at 1.6 miles, then climbs to Copper Lake (4.2 miles, about 2,400 ft of gain) and continues past Little Heart Lake to Big Heart Lake (7.3 miles, about 3,300 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From Big Heart, go cross-country over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake, to Chetwoot Lake, the usual camp. From Chetwoot, climb talus and heather toward Point 6077, pass it on the east through more talus, and gain Iron Cap's west ridge for easy Class 3 scrambling. A short third-class downclimb drops into a notch; beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, without sidehilling, to the broad north ridge, and easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the 6,347 ft summit. A variation climbs from the Iron Cap Lake outlet on ledges around the nose of the north ridge. Route-finding through the boulder fields is the crux of the approach: cairns are sparse, and a map or GPS track is strongly advised. Most parties take two to three days, about 24 miles round trip.
keptBefore.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent or loops through the Iron Cap Lake basin. From the summit, follow the broad north ridge down on easy red-tinged rock and dirt, then either return across the ramp and up out of the notch onto the west ridge and down the talus to Chetwoot Lake, or continue down the north ridge to Iron Cap Lake and work back to camp through the lake basin. This is a Class 2-3 walk-off with no fixed anchors or rappels. The main hazards are loose dirt over rock, especially when wet or with snow patches early in the season, and picking the wrong line: parties who lose the ramp or wander east end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands or in steep heather, so retrace your ascent track. From Chetwoot, reverse the cross-country leg over Atrium Ridge to Big Heart Lake and walk the West Fork Foss trail about 7.3 miles back to the trailhead.
keptBefore.bail: Retreat is straightforward at nearly any point on the ridge or the cross-country approach by simply reversing the ascent line back to Chetwoot Lake and the maintained trail — no fixed rappels or technical retreat gear are needed.

itinerary.cal: The lake basins and the ridge typically aren't snow-free until mid-to-late July, so August-September is the most reliable window.

days.note: From the West Fork Foss trailhead, follow Trail 1064 past Trout, Copper and Little Heart lakes to Big Heart Lake, where the trail ends, then go cross-country over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past Little Chetwoot Lake, to camp at Chetwoot Lake. The trail miles are steady; the off-trail leg is slow.

climate.typical: Wet, cool west-slope Cascades climate; heavy winter snowpack persists into early summer, especially on north-facing terrain. Reliable snow-free scrambling conditions typically arrive by late July/August and hold through September.

bySeason.fall: Late September into October: shorter days and rising storm risk; snow can return to the high basin by mid-October.
bySeason.spring: Not viable — approach trail and route are largely snow-covered with high avalanche hazard on surrounding slopes during May-June snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Best window (August-September): warm, mostly snow-free ridge, though the boulder-field approach still demands care and route-finding.
bySeason.winter: The Foss River roads and the trail are typically snow-covered and effectively inaccessible; not a winter objective.

weather.typical: Maritime Cascades climate; the route window is the driest and clearest in mid-to-late summer, with full snow cover in winter and lingering snow/avalanche risk in spring
weather.probability: Afternoon convective showers are a general Cascades summer pattern; no route-specific thunderstorm frequency data was found for Iron Cap

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Class 3 terrain on loose talus and short rock steps (on-file hazard: loose rock); parties describe a short 3rd-class downclimb near a notch adding fall exposure, and the long, unmaintained approach (on-file hazard: long approach) increases the consequence of any injury given distance from help

approach_variants.name: Iron Cap Lake basin to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: However you reach it, the last of the walking is cross-country over open talus, heather benches and scree above the lake basin. Route-finding is the crux of the approach rather than any move on it: the ground is unmarked and lightly cairned, the footing is loose rock and dirt with occasional steep heather, and visibility-dependent cliff bands will stop a poorly chosen line. Water is scarce once you leave the valley floor, so tank up before the final push.
hazards: Loose dirt over rock on the upper slopes
Steep heather with poor runout
Cliff bands on the east side that will stop a badly chosen line
Snow lingering into early July on north-facing ground
No water above the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling begins on rock ledges above the outlet of Iron Cap Lake. Cross the outlet stream and start working upward to the southeast on a series of ledges — the change from vegetated, dirt-over-rock ground to continuous clean ledges is the tell that you are on the route, and the rock here is genuinely solid, unlike everything below it. The line curves around the nose of the north ridge rather than attacking the summit block head-on. Higher, a short third-class downclimb drops into a notch, which reads as a dead end and is not one: beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, taking you across without sidehilling, and meets the broad north ridge. From there easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the true summit. Losing that ramp is the way parties end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands, so note the line as you go and retrace it exactly on the way down.

climbing_route.notes: Gained from Chetwoot Lake over unmarked talus and heather toward Point 6077, passing it on the east; loose rock and dirt underfoot with occasional steep heather. Class 2-3 scrambling toward the 6,347 ft summit.

climbing_route.label: Ramp below the summit block to the north ridge
climbing_route.notes: Beyond the notch a wide ramp traverses below the summit block — no sidehilling required — to meet the broad north ridge, which is easy red-rock and dirt scrambling to the true summit.
